study.title: Joshua 4 - Memoria of miracle and testimony to the nations
study.overview: Joshua 4 narrates the crossing of the Jordan, and above all the way God commands to preserve his memory among the people. Twelve stones are removed from the riverbed and placed in Gilgal as a pedagogical sign for future generations. The chapter also shows the obedience of Joshua, the participation of the tribes of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh, the public confirmation of Joshua's leadership, and the return of the waters to their normal course. The final purpose stated is that the Lord's strong hand be known to all and that Israel has continually feared it.

outline.title: The Twelve Stones as a Memorial
outline.explanation: After all the nation is going through, the Lord commands twelve men to bring twelve stones out of the Jordan. These stones should serve as a sign for the future: when the children asked what they meant, the parents should tell that the Lord opened the river for the people to pass. The memorial is not just visual memory; it is an instrument of teaching about God's saving action.

outline.title: The complete crossing and the honor given to Joshua
outline.explanation: In addition to the stones taken to Gilgal, Joshua also erects a memorial in the middle of the Jordan. The priests remain standing still until everything is fulfilled, and the people pass hastily. The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh pass armed in front of the others. On that day the LORD magnifies Joshua before all Israel, and the people fear him as Moses had feared.

outline.title: The ark rises and the waters return
outline.explanation: The Lord commands that the priests go up from the Jordan, and when they go out of the bed, the waters return immediately to their place. The people then cross and camp in Gilgal, on the east side of Jericho. The text emphasizes that the change in the waters takes place under the rule of God, represented by the ark of the covenant.

outline.title: Memorial in Gilgal and universal purpose
outline.explanation: The twelve stones are erected in Gilgal and associated with the teaching of children. The narrative concludes with the theological explanation of the sign: Israel crossed dry because the Lord dried up the Jordan, just as he had done in the Red Sea. The goal is for all peoples to know the strong hand of the Lord and that Israel will have the theme every day.

study.context: The chapter continues the narrative of Israel's entry into the promised land. The text mentions the priests who bear the ark of the covenant or testimony, the tribes that had already received previous guidance from Moses, and the camp at Gilgal near Jericho. The notes also highlight that the crossing was extraordinary and that the waters returned to their normal course only after the priests left the river.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God acts historically, visible and memorablely to form the faith of his people. The stones function as a memorial and as domestic catechesis: faith must depend not only on individual memory, but rather be transmitted to generations. The obedience of Joshua shows dependence on the divine direction, not autonomous initiative. Joshua's exaltation is not an end in itself, but confirms before Israel that God guides his people through legitimate leadership. Finally, the miracle has a missionary horizon: the Lord's strong hand must be known among the peoples, and the fear of God must last every day. The repetition of the dry crossing, in parallel with the Red Sea, emphasizes that the God of the exodus continues to act in favor of his people.

scholarViews.insight: The stones were a memorial and also a teaching resource for future generations to ask and receive explanation about the work of God.
The chapter highlights how Joshua executed exactly what God commanded him, without acting on his own, showing fidelity to divine direction.
The declared purpose of the sign reaches not only Israel, but also the peoples of the earth, so that they may know the mighty action of God.

questions: What concrete memories of God's action in your life or in the life of your community do you preserve to teach others?
Have you answered the facts of God's grace with daily reverent fear, how does the chapter command?
How can your family or church turn God's testimony into an intentional conversation with the next generations?
study.practice: Take a time to tell, with simple and faithful words, a specific work that God has done in your life or in the history of your church. Do this with the goal of teaching someone younger in the faith. Then also practice immediate obedience: choose a clear biblical order that you have postponed and answer it this week with concrete action.
study.uncertainty: Clarke's notes suggest that the expression translated "all the peoples of the earth" may refer more immediately to the Canaanite nations; but the biblical text in Portuguese has a broader reach. It is also not possible to confirm, only with these notes, the exact physical form of the memorial in Gilgal or in the middle of the Jordan.
